summary.text: Front cover of the World Health Organization brochure "Understanding National Health Workforce Accounts".

sections.title: Page 2

summary.text: Defines National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) as a system of core indicators and data characteristics designed to standardize health workforce information systems, improve data quality and comparability, and track human resources for health (HRH) policy performance towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC).

sections.extract: + 2 + 1. What is National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA)? The purpose of the NHWA is to facilitate the standardization of a health workforce information system in order to improve data quality, as well as to support tracking HRH policy performance towards Universal Health Coverage (UHC). The NHWA is built up of core indicators and data characteristics that can be progressively measured in order: • generate

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Outlines the national, regional, and global relevance of engaging in NHWA, listing seven core benefits including understanding workforce equity and gaps, informing education scale-up and intersectoral dialogue across health, education, and finance ministries, guiding priority investments, and fostering cross-country data comparability.

sections.extract: + 3 + • A better understanding of the health workforce, including equity and gaps. • Generating quality evidence to inform policy decisions according to country needs. • Ability to guide and inform the transformation and scale-up of health workforce education and training in support of UHC. • Inform intersectoral policy dialogue among the relevant ministries (e.g. education, health and finance). • Inform priority

sections.title: Page 4

summary.text: Presents the global policy rationale and mandate for NHWA within the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (specifically SDG target 3.c on health financing and health workforce recruitment, training, and retention) and the recommendations of the High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth.

sections.extract: + 4 + 3. The 2030 Agenda gives recognition to UHC as key to achieving all other health targets. SDG 3c sets a target to “substantially increase health financing and the recruitment, development, training and retention of the health workforce in developing countries, especially in least developed countries and small island developing States”. The report of the High Level Commission for Health Employment and Economic

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Describes the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH) and World Health Assembly resolution WHA69.19 (May 2016), which urges Member States to consolidate core HRH data for annual reporting to the Global Health Observatory and progressively implement NHWA.

sections.extract: + 5 + WHO and its partners developed the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 (GSHRH) to accelerate progress towards UHC and the SDGs by ensuring equitable access to health workers within strengthened health systems. sections.title: Page 6

summary.text: Introduces the major health workforce policy questions that NHWA helps answer, covering (1) workforce profile (availability, accessibility, acceptability, and competencies), (2) production and deployment trends, and (3) distribution and productivity gaps by occupation, equity, and skill mix.

sections.extract: + 6 + 4. The NHWA can contribute to finding answers to the following major policy questions related to current HRH challenges and how to optimize planning: 1. Profile: Is the current health workforce available, accessible, acceptable and of the appropriate competencies to provide good quality health services? 2. sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Explains why NHWA uses a health labour market analysis approach, capturing the interplay of four policy domains—workforce production, inflows and outflows, maldistribution and inefficiencies, and private-sector regulation—in achieving equitable access to quality health services.

sections.extract: + 8 + 5. Why a Labour Market analysis approach? The NHWA uses a Labour Market analysis framework. sections.title: Page 10

summary.text: Summarizes the stepwise development of the NHWA handbook and indicators through global expert consultations and Technical Advisory Group workshops at WHO headquarters, selecting indicators based on relevance, availability, and national utilization aligned with the health labour market framework.

sections.extract: + 10 + How was the NHWA handbook developed? 6. The NHWA indicators was developed through a stepwise process that included several phases of consultation with experts from around the world, including deans of faculty, academics, teaching instructors, information systems experts, policy planners, and health professionals from both developed and developing countries. sections.title: Page 11

summary.text: Describes the structure of the NHWA handbook across 10 modules, each containing policy-relevant numeric and capability indicators covering health workforce regulation, management mechanisms, and HRH monitoring systems.

sections.extract: + 11 + How is the NHWA handbook structured? Each of the 10 modules contains a set of indicators with declared policy relevance. These include both numeric and capability indicators that can provide information on regulation and other mechanisms related to the health workforce, and the status of the HRH monitoring and management system. 7.

sections.title: Page 12

summary.text: Illustrates the 10 modules of the NHWA organized across three overarching domains—Education (Modules 2–4: workforce in education, regulation, and finances), Labour Force (Modules 1 and 5–7: active stock, labour market flows, employment conditions, and spending/remuneration), and Serving Population Health Needs (Modules 8–9: skill mix and performance/productivity)—supported by Module 10 on governance, information systems, and planning.

sections.extract: 10 modules of the NHWA Serving Population Health Needs Labour Force Education Module 2 Health workforce in education Module 7 Health workforce spending and remuneration Module 6 Employment characteristics and working conditions Module 5 Health labour market flows Module 1 Active health workforce stock Module 8 Skill mix compositions for models of care Module 9 Performance and productivity Module 10 Health workforce
